answer: Arabs conquered it in the 630s; Arabic and Islam spread gradually, mostly by conversion. Muslims and Christians were the large majority in each count: about 94 percent in 1917, 73 percent Muslim in 1931, 1,203,000 of 1,846,000 settled in 1946. Joan Peters argued for substantial immigration; Porath and Gilmour argued her key figures were wrong. The UN's 1947 committee found Arab growth almost entirely natural. McCarthy found the evidence for it minimal, allowing a rise of one eighth over 50 or 75 years would have gone unnoticed; Gottheil estimates up to 38.7 percent of 1922-31 Arab growth in one region, partly internal movement. Foster dates the first Arab use of 'Palestinian' to 1909, Khalidi the national identity to 1917-23 (noting older ties), Karsh says dispersal after 1948 prevented a cohesive one. Gerber and Fishman (reported by Foster and Tezcan) place it earlier; Khalidi says most Palestinians descend from long-resident people.

facts.text: Joan Peters's 1984 book From Time Immemorial argued that a substantial Arab immigration took place in the first half of the 20th century. Reviewers found her use of statistics and sources unreliable: even Daniel Pipes, who accepted her thesis, said the book 'quotes carelessly, uses statistics sloppily, and ignores inconvenient facts', and Yehoshua Porath and Ian Gilmour argued that her key figures and her reading of the Hope Simpson report were wrong.

facts.text: The UN Special Committee on Palestine (1947) said the Arab population increased 'almost entirely' through births exceeding deaths, and Porath cited the British statistical abstracts for the same conclusion; even Fred Gottheil's own model, which applies a 2.5 percent natural growth rate to the 1922 Muslim population, explains 97.6 percent of the 1931 count (about 735,800 of 753,800), leaving about 18,000 of the 165,000 growth (about 11 percent) unexplained by natural increase. Gottheil adds that the 97.6 percent fit does not prove illegal immigration was small, because the census could not count it.

facts.text: Estimates of Arab immigration differ and use different bases. McCarthy writes that real evidence for Muslim immigration into Palestine is 'minimal' and that immigration after the 1870s was small; he allows that a slow rise of one eighth of the Arab population over 50 or 75 years would not have been noticeable in the rates of increase, but says thousands of Arabs arriving each year 'stretches the limits of credulity', and concludes that the vast majority of the Palestinian Arabs of 1947 were the children of Arabs already living there before modern Jewish immigration began. Gottheil reports that McCarthy used Roberto Bachi's figure of about 900 illegal Arab immigrants a year in 1931-45, and argues that this counts only those discovered by the authorities. Gottheil estimates that Arab movement into the sub-districts that became Israel was as much as 38.7 percent of the 1922-31 Arab growth there, but says the total is unknown and the figure includes Arabs moving within Palestine; Bachi himself wrote, as Gottheil quotes him, that total immigration could not even be guessed.

facts.text: Some historians place Palestinian territorial and group consciousness well before the 20th century. Second-hand: Zachary Foster, quoting Haim Gerber, reports that Gerber reads 17th-century legal opinions that use 'Filastin' and 'biladuna' (our country) 'in senses that go far beyond mere objective geography'; Selim Tezcan reports that Louis Fishman and Gerber place a distinct Palestinian identity in the years before 1914 (Gerber's and Fishman's own texts were not read). First-hand: Rashid Khalidi writes that most Palestinians are descended from people who have lived there for many centuries if not many millennia; the same passage says most Israeli Jews came from Europe and the Arab countries relatively recently, and that they have a deeply felt and ancient religious connection to the country.

contested.text: Whether a 'Palestinian people' existed before the 20th century is a question about when a national identity formed, which historians date differently. Foster: the word first used in 1909. Khalidi: the national identity formed in 1917-23, but on older attachments (a religious tie to Palestine as a holy land, felt before 1914 by Muslims and Christians). Nassar: its particularity was rooted in conditions that preceded Zionist settlement, and it crystallized in the encounter with it. Karsh: after 1948 it was never cohesive.

could_not_verify: Joan Peters's own text: the book is not readable online; her words are quoted from a critic's review (Said, MERIP) and Pipes's summary, so what 'Peters writes' rests on one hostile quotation with ellipses.
The Journal of Palestine Studies article that puts natural increase at 96 percent of Muslim growth in 1922-45: the PDF returns 403 and was not read.
Gerber's and Fishman's own texts, and a Palestinian historian's own statement of identity before 1900 (Doumani, Masalha): only Foster's and Tezcan's reports of them were read.
Bachi's own estimates of Arab immigration (the 900 a year caught illegally): read only through Gottheil and McCarthy.

The census facts (1922, 1931) and the 1946 estimate are now worded as what the record says. The records read are the Survey of Palestine vol. I (a 1946 Government of Palestine publication, scan at bjpa.org), the Mandate government's report on the UN site, and the UN committee's report. The census volumes themselves are lending-library scans and were not read; the readers are the Economic Cooperation Foundation database and the Center for Online Judaic Studies summary of the 1931 census, the Jewish Telegraphic Agency (1922), and for 1946 DellaPergola and Imseis. Whether the censuses are right is a separate question (the Bedouin and women and children are said to be undercounted); a person should read the census volumes (HathiTrust, JSTOR) and McCarthy's tables.

The end-1946 Arab figure is the UN committee's estimate, read by Imseis and in DellaPergola's different 1947 estimate (built on Bachi's, i.e. the same Mandate statistics); no independent count exists.
Facts that do not meet the gate's source rule: none by count. Facts 2, 3 and 4 meet the record rule, but they are the Mandate government's figures, read by sources that copy them.

FINAL REVIEW (2026-11-20): record facts 2 and 3 (1922 and 1931 censuses) are worded as what the census says, the record (the Survey of Palestine, the Mandate report) was read, and the readers (the Economic Cooperation Foundation database, the Jewish Telegraphic Agency, the Center for Online Judaic Studies summary of the 1931 volume) report the same figures. Fact 4 (end-1946 estimate): only Imseis reads the same UNSCOP figure; DellaPergola's 1947 estimate and the Survey's end-1944 figures are different numbers, not readers, and the Jewish Virtual Library only reproduces the text. A person should find a second reader of UNSCOP's 1,203,000 / 608,000 / 35,000. McCarthy's immigration analysis is about Ottoman registers after the 1870s as much as the Mandate years; the Mandate-period dispute is Gottheil's critique of his use of Bachi.
not_claimed: That Palestinian national identity is ancient, or that it is recent: historians disagree on the date, and the card reports the positions.
That no Arab immigration into Mandate Palestine happened: some did, and the size is uncertain.
That the length of time a people has had a national identity decides its rights or the outcome of any modern political question.
That Jews do not have a historical tie to the land: see the Jewish presence card.

skeptic.notes: Final review after the record rule. Read: the Survey of Palestine vol. I (1922: 'total population of 757,182, of 78% were moslems, 11% jews and 9.6% christians'; the 1922/1931 table; OCR gives 73,014 Christians where ECF and JTA give 73,024), the Mandate report, UNSCOP (1,203,000 etc.; 'settled'; Muslim share 75 to 60 percent; 'increased almost entirely' natural), ECF, COJS, McCarthy (the 'minimal', 'small', one-eighth and 'credulity' passages), Gottheil (Bachi's 900 a year counts only those discovered), Khalidi (1997 chapter and 2020 book), Foster, Pipes, Gilmour. Record flags: facts 2 and 3 are honest (worded as what the census says, two real readers each). Fact 4 is worded as what UNSCOP says (honest wording) but has one real reader, so it does not meet the record rule in substance although the gate passes it (must-fix). Fixed by me: (must-fix, done) fact 8 said McCarthy found immigration 'near zero' for Palestine as a whole; his text says evidence is 'minimal' and Muslim immigration after the 1870s 'small', and his one-eighth remark is a hypothetical; reworded, with Gottheil's critique that Bachi's 900 a year counts only discovered entrants. (should-fix, done) fact 5 quoted Khalidi's 'where before no such thing had existed' without his next paragraph, which lists earlier religious attachment to Palestine as a holy land; added. (should-fix, done) fact 6 and the answer said Porath and Gilmour 'showed' Peters wrong, which Pipes disputes; now 'argued'. Still open: (should-fix) Peters is read only through critics and one defender; Gerber and Fishman only through Foster and Tezcan; (should-fix) ECF is an Israeli NGO database labelled reference; (nit) the answer's '1,203,000 of 1,846,000' is one UN estimate. Heard (Gingrich, Meir, Pipes, Peters) is the strong version. Strongest objection, Palestinian: no Palestinian historian is quoted on identity before 1900 in his own words except Khalidi. Jewish: Peters's case appears only through critics. Status stays draft.
